1#main: The law of bones — whether they combine to nullify a forbidden item, and not to nullify a forbidden item l'chatchila. In it are 7 seifim: A piece of nevelah that has meat and bones that fell into a pot of permitted food — the bones of the forbidden item combine with the permitted food to nullify the forbidden item; and needless to say that bones of permitted food combine with permitted food. But the marrow in forbidden bones combines with the forbidden item, and the body of the pot itself does not combine neither with the forbidden item nor with the permitted food: {Rama: And some are stringent not to combine forbidden bones with permitted food to nullify (a hagahah in Sh"D in the name of Or Zarua); and in a place of loss one may rely on those who are lenient and permit, for such is the essential ruling:}
2#main: In what matters is this stated — that forbidden bones combine with permitted food when a piece of nevelah fell into a pot of permitted food while it was raw; but if it was cooked first and afterward fell into a pot of permitted food, the bones in it combine with the forbidden item, because they absorbed from the meat of the nevelah when it was cooked alone:
3#main: In other prohibitions besides basar b'chalav, a piece that absorbed forbidden food combines to nullify the forbidden item: {Rama: And we do not practice thus, for we establish that in all prohibitions a piece becomes nevelah, as above siman 92:}
4#main: We estimate in gravy, kafa (meaning: the very fine particles of meat and spice that collect at the sides of the pot), and pieces; and we estimate the permitted and forbidden food as it appears before us, even though there was more permitted at first and it diminished through cooking and was absorbed in the pot — and this is in not its kind in its kind; but if it is its kind in its kind, we also estimate what the pot absorbed and stands on the walls of the pot, and we estimate this with a good estimate and view it as if it were visible; but what was entirely consumed by the fire does not combine, for it is entirely lost:
5#main: One does not nullify a forbidden item l'chatchila; and even if a forbidden item fell into permitted food that does not have enough measure to nullify it, one does not add permitted food in order to nullify it. If one transgressed and nullified it, or increased permitted food upon it — if b'shogeg it is permitted; if b'mezid it is forbidden for the one who nullifies it himself if it is his, and likewise for one for whom it was nullified (and a forbidden item that was nullified through a non-Jew's action is permitted, as below seif 7):
6#main: A rabbinic prohibition — one does not mix it by hand in order to nullify it; and if one did so b'mezid it is forbidden. But if it fell by itself and there is not enough permitted food to nullify it, one increases permitted food and nullifies it: {Rama: And some say one may not nullify a d'rabbanan prohibition or add to it as with a d'oraisa prohibition, and so is the essential practice (Beit Yosef in the name of Rashba and Tur and Hagahot Maimoniyot and Semag and Hagahat Or Zarua and Mordechai and Ran and Hagahot ShaDa).}
7#main: If a small amount of forbidden food was absorbed into a permitted vessel — if it is the way of that vessel to be used abundantly with permitted food, it is permitted to use it l'chatchila, since the forbidden amount is small and it cannot come to impart taste; therefore a slight forbidden item that was absorbed in a pot or inside jugs and the like is permitted to use l'chatchila with the same kind, and one need not kasher the vessel; and this is when it is not ben yomo (Tur). And if it is ben yomo, it is forbidden l'chatchila to cook in it even the same kind, until one kasher it (there in the name of Semak). And if one cooked in it b'dieved, it is permitted (Mordechai and Ran and Rashba and Tur and Beit Yosef). And some forbid even b'dieved (Hagahot Or Zarua and Semag); and the first view is primary.
